title: Core Software Design Principles
description: Essential software design heuristics: DRY, KISS, YAGNI, Law of Demeter (Least Knowledge), Separation of Concerns, and Encapsulating What Varies.

topics.title: DRY, KISS, and YAGNI
topics.description: Don't Repeat Yourself, Keep It Simple Stupid, and You Aren't Gonna Need It.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: DRY: Every piece of knowledge must have a single authoritative representation. KISS: Simple designs are easier to maintain than clever complex designs. YAGNI: Do not implement features until they are actually needed.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Over-engineering and code duplication are the two primary causes of technical debt and maintenance nightmares.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Write the simplest code that solves today's requirements. Extract common logic to prevent copy-paste bugs.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Avoid speculative generality (e.g. building a multi-tenant plugin engine when only single-user support is required).

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Reusable validation logic avoiding duplicate regexes across registration and profile updates.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Every production software development lifecycle.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Apply KISS and YAGNI constantly during system design interviews.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not over-apply DRY to coincidentally similar code that serves different domain purposes.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Clean, readable, concise code with minimal bugs.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Premature DRY can create artificial coupling between distinct business domains.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: DRY (Knowledge duplication vs accidental duplication).

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Building complex generic abstractions for features that never get used.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: When should you violate DRY?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: When two pieces of code look identical today but belong to different business domains and will evolve for completely different reasons (accidental duplication).

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Refactor duplicated tax calculation into a shared helper.

practice.title: DRY Pricing Calculation
practice.problemStatement: Refactor duplicated tax calculation into a shared helper.

referenceCode.code: class Tax { public: static double withTax(double a) { return a * 1.08; } };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering DRY, KISS, and YAGNI is essential for robust Low-Level System Design.

topics.title: Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge)
topics.description: A method should only talk to its immediate friends, avoiding long train-wreck call chains.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: The Law of Demeter (LoD) states that a method of an object may only call methods of: itself, its parameters, objects it creates, or its direct component members. Avoid a.getB().getC().getD().doSomething().

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Train-wreck calls create brittle coupling: changing class C breaks class A even though class A only wanted something from D.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: 'Tell, Don't Ask.' Tell the immediate friend to perform the operation instead of navigating through its internal object graph.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Instead of customer.getWallet().getCard().charge(), write customer.charge(amount).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Train-Wreck Anti-Pattern
callout.text: user.getProfile().getAddress().getGeo().getCoordinates(); // Violates Law of Demeter! Coupling to 4 nested classes!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: StoreRegister communicates only with Customer, remaining ignorant of Wallet internals.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Microservice domain boundaries and object-oriented encapsulation.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use LoD to minimize ripple effects when internal object structures change.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not apply LoD to fluent builders (e.g. QueryBuilder.select().from() where each method returns *this).

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Loose coupling and high maintainability.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: May require creating forwarding methods on container classes.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Tell Don't Ask, Method forwarding.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Reaching into nested getters across multiple layers.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: Why is a.getB().getC().doAction() a violation of the Law of Demeter?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: Because class A now directly depends on the internal navigation structure of B and C. If B's internal representation changes, class A breaks.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Refactor PaperBoy taking money from Customer's Wallet into Customer.pay(amount).

practice.title: Refactor PaperBoy LoD
practice.problemStatement: Refactor PaperBoy taking money from Customer's Wallet into Customer.pay(amount).

referenceCode.code: class Customer { Wallet w; public: bool pay(double a) { return w.deduct(a); } };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge) is essential for robust Low-Level System Design.

topics.title: Separation of Concerns & Modularity
topics.description: Dividing a software application into distinct features that overlap in functionality as little as possible.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Separation of Concerns (SoC) is the software design principle of breaking an architecture into distinct sections, where each section addresses a separate concern (e.g. Presentation, Business Logic, Persistence).

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Mixing database queries, UI rendering, and business calculations in a single function makes code unmaintainable.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Each module has a dedicated role: Model represents business state, View renders UI, Controller coordinates user interaction.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Organize code into clear architectural tiers (MVC, Clean Architecture, Hexagonal Ports & Adapters).

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Architectural Tiers
callout.text: UI Layer -> Business Service Layer -> Data Access Layer -> Storage

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Clean separation between database retrieval and business transfer validation.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Enterprise web backends, financial trading systems, desktop applications.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use layered architecture in all non-trivial systems.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not create excessive tiers for simple CRUD utilities.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Independent team development, testability, and technology swap freedom.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Requires passing data transfer objects across layer boundaries.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: MVC, MVP, MVVM, Clean Architecture.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Writing raw SQL queries inside UI click event handlers.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does Separation of Concerns relate to Single Responsibility Principle?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: SoC is a high-level system architectural principle (separating UI, logic, data layers), while SRP is the class-level object-oriented realization of SoC.

topics.title: Encapsulate What Varies & Favor Immutability
topics.description: Identify the aspects of your application that vary and separate them from what stays the same.

sections.title: 1. What is it?
sections.content: Encapsulate What Varies is a core design heuristic: identify the parts of a system that change frequently and encapsulate them behind an interface to protect stable parts.

sections.title: 2. Why do we need it?
sections.content: Prevents constant churn and regression testing across the entire system when business rules change.

sections.title: 3. Core idea
sections.content: Isolate the moving parts behind interfaces (Strategy / Factory patterns) and make static parts immutable.

sections.title: 4. How it works
sections.content: Extract dynamic algorithms into polymorphic classes. Mark unchanged state const.

sections.title: 5. Visual explanation
sections.content: Visual Architecture & Mechanics:

callout.title: Core Heuristic
callout.text: Take what varies and 'encapsulate' it so it won't affect the rest of your code!

sections.title: 6. C++ implementation
sections.content: Complete Production C++20 Implementation:

sections.title: 7. Code walkthrough
sections.content: Pricing volatility is encapsulated in strategy classes; RideBooking workflow stays stable.

sections.title: 8. Real-world example
sections.content: Ride-sharing surge pricing, airline ticketing, dynamic insurance underwriting.

sections.title: 9. When to use
sections.content: Use whenever business policies, algorithms, or integrations vary frequently.

sections.title: 10. When NOT to use
sections.content: Do not encapsulate aspects that are guaranteed never to change.

sections.title: 11. Advantages
sections.content: Protects core workflow stability; enables zero-risk runtime algorithm swapping.

sections.title: 12. Disadvantages
sections.content: Increases class count.

sections.title: 13. Variations / Types
sections.content: Strategy Pattern, Policy-based Design, Immutability.

sections.title: 14. Common mistakes
sections.content: Hardcoding varying calculation rules inside main business classes.

sections.title: 15. Interview questions
sections.content: Q: How does 'Encapsulate What Varies' lead directly to the Strategy Design Pattern?

sections.title: 16. Interview answer
sections.content: Answer: When algorithm variations are extracted into separate classes implementing a common interface, that structure IS the Strategy Design Pattern.

sections.title: 17. Practice problem
sections.content: Encapsulate state-by-state tax calculation variation.

referenceCode.code: class ITaxRule { public: virtual ~ITaxRule() = default; virtual double tax(double) = 0; };

sections.title: 18. Summary
sections.content: Mastering Encapsulate What Varies & Favor Immutability is essential for robust Low-Level System Design.
